headline: Small programs. Bodies you can explore.
lede: A Quineling gives a small program a mathematical body. Close a road or change a water reading, then run it and follow the result through the creature’s parts.
labTitle: Change an input. Follow the result.
labIntro: Choose an example, load the suggested change, then run the comparison. Both sets of inputs go through the same program, keeping its source and body unchanged. Select a highlighted operation to inspect its values before and after.
replayIntro: “Replay this request” retrieves the same saved run record, so you see the same output and recorded operation values. It runs no task and does not animate the trace. “Run the comparison” evaluates both input sets again, creating new records for accepted inputs even when the values are unchanged.
ownershipIntro: The body is a visual representation of the program. Its curves and dimensions come from the source, which assigns each region to an operation. This assignment is called ownership: selecting the operation highlights its region. For example, the water total owns a band around the trunk. Operation names do not prescribe unique shapes, so different programs can look alike.
bodyLegend: Colors group operations by role, so two operations can share a color. Gold labels show values from a run that matches the current source and inputs, while gold lines trace the selected operation’s input connections. Playing the gesture changes the pose without running the task.
metricsHelp: These measurements describe the displayed comparison. “Changed node values” counts differences in recorded operation values. “Source identity” checks whether both runs used the same source. “Anatomy change” reports the root mean square (RMS) distance between corresponding body points at a fixed gesture phase; zero means those points did not move. The separate “Interpreter requests” count totals requests to evaluate tasks across this page, including inputs it rejects. A normal comparison adds two requests. Replay, gesture playback and passive genome decoding add none; recovering and running three copies adds three.
sourceTitle: Give the program a new rule.
sourceIntro: With the prepared readings of 1.5, 5 and 0.5 liters, a five-liter cap lowers the total from 7 to 5. The graph grows from four operations to five, and the source assigns the new operation a band around the trunk. Both bodies keep the same four connected parts, with different dimensions and assignments of regions to operations.
retryIntro: For the prepared outcomes “retry, retry, ok,” a cap of one stops after the first entry; a cap of four reaches “ok” on the third. Compare the four-attempt policy with a cap of your choice. Each cap is part of that program’s source. The calculation reviews supplied outcomes and submits no work.
quineTitle: Check the source. Recover a runnable copy.
quineIntro: A quine emits its own complete source. “Verify source” runs the constructor and checks that its emitted source matches the original exactly, without evaluating the task.
conceptBody: The “thought” is the author’s public description of a task. The source declares a finite, typed graph: each operation accepts specified kinds of input and passes its result along the connections. The same source assigns regions of the body to operations. Select one to locate its tissue and inspect its connections.
thoughtBody: The calculation runs locally, and any action receipts are simulations. The public description is not a window into a model’s private reasoning. Animation gives the creature a living appearance; it has no awareness or independent intentions.
noveltyTitle: Why give a program a body?
noveltyBody: The calculations use familiar methods, including sums and shortest-path search. A runnable task and its inspectable body share one source that can reconstruct itself. Use the body to locate an operation and the run record to see what it computed. Different programs can look alike; exact identity comes from source bytes.
furtherTitle: Build a task of your own.
furtherBody: Use the QDL 1 workspace to author typed programs and supply new inputs. Agents can use the SDK’s MCP and A2A adapters. The Ranch explores program composition and body inheritance under experimental rules.
genomeIntro: A genome is another encoding of those source bytes: harmonic data stores them in wave coefficients; RGB data stores them as exact red, green and blue values. Decoding reads the complete records, not the portrait, and runs no task.
generationIntro: A generation is a fresh program built from the previous program’s emitted source. “Recover and run three generations” builds that chain through source, harmonic data and RGB data. Each copy runs with the same recorded inputs in a fresh session, and its source and result are checked against the original. Earlier run history is not restored.
